title: One reason to change
idea: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) says a class should have one reason to change: it serves one actor, so one team's request cannot break another's.

analogy.text: A restaurant keeps its menu designer and its accountant apart. A new menu font never changes how the till adds tax to the bill.
analogy.breaks: People split by job title; classes split by who requests changes.

points: An actor is one team or role that asks for changes to the code.
Group code that changes for one reason; split code with different reasons.
Symptom: unrelated tickets keep editing one file, and each fix breaks another feature.
In interviews, name each class's actor aloud before adding a method to it.

hero.title: Each team owns exactly one rule

steps.caption: `CheckoutService` only sequences the steps. It changes when the checkout flow changes, not when a rule does.
It books the net total in `Ledger`. Only accounting decides how that class works.
It asks `ReceiptFormatter` for the customer's text. Layout requests land here and nowhere else.
The formatter asks `VatCalculator` for the gross price. It uses the tax rule but does not own it.
A new VAT rule edits only `VatCalculator`. Receipts pick it up; the ledger stays net.
Each rule has one owning team. `CheckoutService` changes only when the checkout flow itself changes. That map is SRP made visible.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: One `Order` class serves three teams. A harmless receipt request corrupts the books.

walk.text: Pricing, receipt layout and bookkeeping all live in one class, sharing one list.
The receipt team wanted VAT-inclusive prices, so someone edited the shared `totalCents()`.
The receipt now shows the gross amount. The request that drove the edit is met.
Bookkeeping reuses the same method, so VAT is silently booked as revenue.
Compare the ledger with what accounting expects. It compiles and runs; only the numbers are wrong.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Split by actor: each class has one owner, and `CheckoutService` only wires them.

walk.text: `Order` is an immutable record that rejects negative prices. Its net total is the fact every team shares.
`VatCalculator` owns the tax rule and rejects a negative rate. Only finance changes it.
`ReceiptFormatter` builds the customer's text from the gross price. Layout changes stop here.
`Ledger` books net revenue and returns a copy, never its internal list.
`CheckoutService` gets collaborators by constructor injection. It decides step order, no business rules.
Now the receipt shows VAT while the ledger stays net. Both teams get what they asked.

pitfalls: Splitting by method count, not by actor, gives tiny classes that still change together.
A `Manager` or `Utils` class that every team edits is a violation; watch its merge conflicts.
Splitting a small script with one owner adds indirection for nothing; wait for a second actor.

quiz.q: After the split, finance changes how VAT is rounded. Which classes change?
quiz.why: Rounding lives in `grossCents`. `ReceiptFormatter` only asks `VatCalculator` for the gross price, and `Ledger` books net, so neither changes.

takeaway: One class, one actor: split when two teams' changes collide.

starters: How do I find the actors of a class I inherited?
Is a service class with many methods always an SRP violation?
How small should a class be before SRP becomes overkill?
